fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the target surface-segregation and active-diffusion mechanism with short-range clustering and lattice distortion without evidence that these govern thermal stability in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt particles.
It predicts improved stability after annealing, opposite to the observed segregation, evaporation, particle loss, and size reduction.
The cited evidence concerns primarily bulk refractory TaNbHfZr HEAs and mechanical properties, so it does not support the extrapolation to noble/transition-metal nanoalloy surface stability.

The proposed experiment measures hardness, strength, and ductility rather than the relevant observables: elemental surface segregation, self-diffusivity, morphology, particle-size distribution, melting, and evaporation.
The before-versus-after baseline cannot distinguish SRC-driven behavior from surface-energy-driven segregation, coalescence, phase separation, or ordinary annealing effects.
explanation: The response is broadly about high-temperature HEAs but does not reconstruct the material, thermal protocol, nanoscale regime, mechanism, or outcomes of the target. Its SRC hypothesis has some basis in the cited TaNbHfZr literature, but those sources establish clustering and mechanical-property evolution in a different refractory alloy system, not enhanced structural or chemical stability in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles. The test is insufficiently controlled and focuses on mechanical properties, so it cannot discriminate the proposed mechanism from the target alternative. Boundaries are named only as generic variables, with no quantitative temperature, size, shape, atmosphere, or time regime. The falsification rule also tests property improvement rather than the asserted causal link between SRC formation and stability.
